title: Checkpoint: How the Internet Works
objective: After this level you can trace a packet from your device through addresses, DNS, routers and cables and explain how it arrives complete.
summary: One request to example.com, start to finish: DNS lookup, TCP handshake, layers of headers, NAT, hop-by-hop routing and light in fiber, with TCP making it complete.

cards.headline: You type example.com and press Enter. What happens before a byte comes back?
cards.body: Chapter 4 finale. Follow one request out of your home and across the internet, and watch each idea from this chapter take its turn.

events.label: DNS: the resolver asks the root, .com, then the owner for the IP address
TCP: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK opens a numbered connection
Layers: the request is wrapped in TCP, IP and link headers
Home router: NAT swaps your private address for its public one
Routers: each sends it one hop on, Time to Live down by one
Fiber: pulses of light carry it along the long stretches

items.label: The switch at home
points: Reads MAC addresses on each frame

cards.headline: Why it arrives complete
cards.body: Nothing in the middle promises anything: IP packets can be lost, repeated or scrambled, and each router only knows its next hop. Completeness comes from the two ends. Before your browser can contact the site at all, DNS must supply its address; after that, TCP numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrived and resends whatever didn't.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How a request finds a server by name, crosses routers hop by hop and arrives complete.
Why IPv4 addresses ran out, and how private addresses and NAT let a whole home share one.
How TCP turns lost, repeated or scrambled packets into a perfect download.
What keeps light inside a fiber, and how homes connect by phone line, cable, glass or satellite.

questions.prompt: On the trip to example.com, what has to happen before your browser can contact the site at all?

options.label: A traceroute of the whole path
options.rationale: Traceroute is a diagnostic tool, not a required step.

options.label: DNS has to supply the site's IP address
The site has to send its page first
options.rationale: The page comes only after you ask for it.

options.label: Every router has to approve the route
options.rationale: Routers just forward packets one hop at a time.

questions.explanation: A browser needs the site's IP address, so the DNS lookup comes first; only then can TCP open a connection.

questions.prompt: How does the page arrive complete when IP in the middle promises nothing?

options.label: The routers check every packet's contents
options.rationale: Routers only forward; they promise nothing.

options.label: Fiber never loses a packet
options.rationale: Any link can lose or damage packets.

options.label: TCP at the two ends numbers, acknowledges and resends
DNS keeps a backup copy of the page

questions.explanation: Completeness is handled at the ends: TCP numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrived and resends what did not.

questions.prompt: Your request passes a switch at home, then routers beyond. Which addresses does each one read?

options.label: Switch: IP address; router: MAC address
options.rationale: It is the other way round.

options.label: Both read only the domain name
options.rationale: Names are turned into addresses before sending.

options.label: Switch: port number; router: sequence number
options.rationale: Those belong to TCP at the two ends.

options.label: Switch: MAC address; router: destination IP address

questions.explanation: Switches forward frames by MAC address inside one network; routers look up the destination IP address to choose the next hop.

questions.prompt: From Level 37: glass fibers of the 1960s lost their light after about how far?

options.label: 20 meters
1 kilometer
options.rationale: Kao hoped just 1 percent would survive a kilometer.

options.label: 100 kilometers
options.rationale: That was what Kao calculated pure glass could reach.

options.label: 6,000 kilometers
options.rationale: Old fibers could not come close.

questions.explanation: Fibers of the 1960s carried light only about 20 meters; Kao calculated the purest glass could reach over 100 kilometers.

questions.prompt: From Level 39: why does a geostationary satellite seem to hover over one spot?

options.label: Engines fire constantly to hold it still in the sky
One lap of its orbit takes as long as one turn of the Earth
A long cable tethers it to a station on the ground
options.rationale: Nothing connects it to the ground but radio.

options.label: It orbits so low that it barely moves across the sky
options.rationale: It orbits 35,786 km up, far above low orbit.

questions.explanation: At 35,786 km, its orbit matches Earth's rotation, so it stays over the same spot.
